details: Babel Fish was a free Web-based machine translation service by Yahoo!. In May 2012 it was replaced by Bing Translator (now Microsoft Translator), to which queries were redirected. Although Yahoo! has transitioned its Babel Fish translation services to Bing Translator, it did not sell its translation application to Microsoft outright. As the oldest free online language translator, the service translated text or Web pages in 36 pairs between 13 languages, including English, Simplified Chinese, Traditional Chinese, Dutch, French, German, Greek, Italian, Japanese, Korean, Portuguese, Russian, and Spanish. The internet service derived its name from the Babel fish, a fictional species in Douglas Adams's book and radio series The Hitchhiker's Guide to the Galaxy that could instantly translate languages. In turn, the name of the fictional creature refers to the biblical account of the confusion of languages that arose in the city of Babel.

explainer.lead: Babel Fish was Yahoo!'s free website for translating text or Web pages between a fixed set of languages. It made machine translation easy for ordinary Web users to try, until it was replaced by Bing Translator in May 2012.

tiers.eli5: Babel Fish was like a language helper on a website: you gave it some writing or a Web page, and it tried to rewrite the words in another language. It was named after a fictional creature in The Hitchhiker's Guide to the Galaxy that could instantly translate languages. In May 2012, its queries began going to Bing Translator instead.
tiers.practitioner: Babel Fish should be treated as a discontinued consumer machine-translation service, not an integration option: queries were redirected to Bing Translator, now Microsoft Translator, in May 2012. It accepted text or Web pages and supported 36 language pairs across 13 languages. Its pair-based coverage meant that having a language on the list did not imply support for translating it into every other listed language.
tiers.paperLevel: Let L be the set of 13 supported languages and P ⊂ L × L the 36 supported language pairs. For each (s,t) ∈ P, Babel Fish provided a machine-translation function M_(s,t): X_s → X_t, where X_s was supplied text or Web-page content in language s and X_t was the translated output in language t. Its coverage was limited to those fixed pairs, and the service was replaced in May 2012.

explainer.example: A visitor could enter an English paragraph and select English–French; Babel Fish would return a French machine translation of that paragraph. Alternatively, the visitor could submit a Web page for translation.

usedIn.name: Yahoo!
usedIn.detail: Provided Babel Fish as a free Web-based machine translation service.

usedIn.name: Online text and Web-page translation
usedIn.detail: Let users submit either text or Web pages for translation between supported language pairs.

usedIn.name: Bing Translator
usedIn.detail: Received redirected Babel Fish queries after replacing the service in May 2012; it is now Microsoft Translator.

explainer.intuition: The idea was to put automatic translation behind a simple Web page: supply writing and choose a supported language pair, then receive a translation. Its name evoked Douglas Adams's fictional Babel fish, which could instantly translate languages.
howItWorks: A user supplied text or a Web page.
The user chose one of the 36 supported pairs among 13 languages.
Babel Fish applied machine translation to produce output in the target language.
After its replacement in May 2012, queries were redirected to Bing Translator.
explainer.whyItMatters: As the oldest free online language translator, Babel Fish gave Web users an early, accessible way to translate text and pages without installing software. Its redirection to Bing Translator also illustrates how a familiar service can survive as an entry point while the underlying service changes.
misconceptions: It was a website and translation service, not the fictional creature from which it took its name.
Yahoo! did not sell its translation application outright to Microsoft.
It did not support every possible translation among its 13 languages; it supported 36 specific pairs.

diagram.caption: Babel Fish originally turned submitted content and a chosen language pair into a translation; after May 2012, its queries went to Bing Translator.
